analysis.title: GS - Coppersmith - US Equities - less risk appetite - 1 Nov 2026
key_insights: Global risk appetite fell sharply in October. GS's Risk Appetite Indicator (RAI) recorded its largest drop since November 2021, but levels are not yet low enough to signal the contrarian buying opportunities of recent years, because the starting point was high.
After the 11 largest RAI declines since 2005, S&P 500 outcomes ranged from -17% to +7% over 1 month and -32% to +18% over 6 months, so tail risk runs in both directions.
Hedge funds had a hard October. Fundamental L/S lost 3.5% and systematic L/S lost 3.6%, including a 2.5% loss last week, the worst since December 2023.

Hedge fund gross exposure is 314%, the 97th percentile over 5 years, while net exposure is in the 10th percentile over 1 year. Fundamental L/S beta-adjusted net fell to a 1-year low. Managers keep cutting market exposure, but high leverage leaves room for more volatility.
Institutions remain short VIX futures but have covered aggressively over the last couple of weeks, nearly matching the covering seen in Q1.

Aggregate earnings are not the problem. With 60% of the S&P 500 reported, EPS growth is tracking +33% y/y and 70% of stocks have risen since earnings season began. The weakness is in the largest, best-owned names, especially hyperscalers, where strong results did not clear a high bar.

The AI debate is shifting from growth to the cost and financing of that growth. Hyperscaler capex is expected to reach $1.2tn in 2027, aggregate FCF turned negative in Q3, and the pace of upward earnings revisions is moderating, in crowded and heavily levered parts of the market.

A GS Research note argues the AI funding gap may be smaller than feared. Oracle plans to spend about $220bn on AI infrastructure but expects to raise only $20bn through 2030, with customers and suppliers sharing the cost. GS Credit estimates the bond market could absorb another ~$500bn of hyperscaler debt.

On AI demand, the next wave is expected from companies using AI across everyday business functions rather than only coding. Microsoft's AI development platform is growing +300% y/y, which suggests adoption is early. The question is shifting to who profits from it.

The Fed was almost a sideshow this week. Warsh struck a measured tone and GIR still expects another hike in December. AI-related equity volatility has overtaken energy as a key driver of bond yields, and the Fed acknowledged part of this.
Investors remain underweight Treasuries, so yields have room to fall further if risk-off continues.

Midterm elections are the focus next week. Democrats are above 90% to take the House. GIR sees limited immediate market implications, since divided government makes major policy changes unlikely. Higher tariffs (about 2 points of effective tariff rate) and fiscal talks around the Dec 11 funding deadline are the bigger risks.

GS thinks fears of a regulatory crackdown on data centers are overdone. Nationwide restrictions look unlikely and political pressure may ease after the election, so Washington looks less likely to derail the AI buildout than feared.

Near-term the author sees reasons to be somewhat more constructive, given earnings are holding up and positioning has reset considerably. Elevated gross leverage and the unresolved AI debate leave room for further volatility, and tail risks in both directions remain unusually large.
